rationale: The hypothesis posits that optic atrophy is uncommon in SPG93 (present in <20%, ≤3/16 patients) and serves as a reliable negative discriminator against other mitochondrial spastic paraplegias like SPG7. However, reviews of iron-sulfur cluster and lipoic acid synthesis disorders involving NFU1 (Tort et al., 2016; Lebigot et al., 2021) and curated genetic databases (GenCC, MedGen, HPO) repeatedly identify optic atrophy as part of the core clinical spectrum in patients with NFU1-related spastic paraplegia, with HPO classifying optic atrophy in SPG93 as frequent. While severe early-onset NFU1 deficiency (MMDS1) is characterized by fatal pulmonary hypertension and encephalopathy where optic atrophy is less emphasized, attenuated forms presenting as hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG93) regularly manifest optic atrophy and peripheral neuropathy.

conflicts: The hypothesis asserts optic atrophy occurs in <20% of SPG93 cases, whereas multiple clinical literature reviews of NFU1 phenotypes (Tort et al. 2016, Lebigot et al. 2021) and HPO annotations classify optic atrophy as a frequent and prominent feature of the NFU1 spastic paraplegia spectrum.

Using the presence of optic atrophy to rule out SPG93 in favor of other mitochondrial HSPs (such as SPG7) is contradicted by clinical evidence demonstrating that optic atrophy frequently co-segregates with NFU1-related spastic paraplegia.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact incidence of subclinical optic neuropathy via optical coherence tomography (OCT) and visual evoked potentials (VEP) across all reported NFU1-SPG93 patients?
new_directions.rationale: Many mitochondrial spastic paraplegias present with subclinical or late-onset optic nerve pallor; systematic ophthalmologic workups would establish true penetrance and discriminative utility.
